Capital per person is our own perpetual-inventory estimate from PWT investment, and TFP is computed from it.
Prepared file: [`data/ch04/pwt_production.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch04/pwt_production.csv) (see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch04/README.md)).
Chart: inspired by Fig. 4.5 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

<!-- cell -->

**What to notice.**

- With $\alpha = 1/3$, almost every country lies far **above** the 45-degree line: the model predicts that
  poor countries should be much richer than they are. Burundi is predicted to have about 1/6 of U.S.
  income, but it actually has about 1/74. The "typical gap" in the title is the median of predicted
  over actual income: the typical country is predicted to be 2.8 times richer than it is.
- The gap shrinks as income rises, and the richest countries lie close to the line.
- Move the exponent to $\alpha = 1$, so that $y = k$. The poor countries now overshoot and fall *below* the
  line: Burundi is predicted at about 1/221 of U.S. income, but it has about 1/74. Most rich countries stay
  above it. Capital's share of income is close to 1/3 in the data, so raising the
  exponent is not a good way to rescue the model.

## Total factor productivity

The model fits much better once productivity can differ across countries. Here we measure that productivity, called TFP, as the part of income that capital does not explain.

<!-- cell -->

### Fig. 6: The U.S. and Chinese production functions

**Goal.** Bring productivity back into the model and measure it.

Countries are poorer than their capital predicts, so they must use their capital and labor less
efficiently: they have a lower $\bar{A}$. We cannot observe $\bar{A}$ directly, but we observe everything else in
equation (7), $y^* = \bar{A}\bar{k}^{1/3}$. So we choose the $\bar{A}$ that makes the equation hold exactly (equation 8):

$$\bar{A} = \frac{y^*}{\bar{k}^{1/3}}$$

This is **total factor productivity (TFP)**. It is already in our data as the column `tfp`. A lower TFP shifts
the whole production function down.

```{python}
def compare_with_us(country="China"):
    """Fig. 4.6: the U.S. production function (A = 1) and another country's (its implied TFP), 2023."""
    row = sample[sample.country == country].iloc[0]
    A, k, y = row.tfp, row.k_rel, row.y_rel
    points = pd.DataFrame({"label": ["U.S.", f"{short(country)} with U.S. TFP", short(country)],
                           "k": [1.0, k, k], "y": [1.0, k ** (1 / 3), y]})
    fig = px.scatter(points, x="k", y="y", text="label", hover_name="label",
                     labels={"k": "Capital per person, k (U.S. = 1)", "y": "Output per person, y (U.S. = 1)"})
    fig.update_traces(marker=dict(color="black", size=12), textposition=["top center", "bottom right", "bottom right"])
    grid = np.linspace(0, 2, 300)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=grid, y=grid ** (1 / 3), name="U.S. production function, A = 1",
                             line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3)))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=grid, y=A * grid ** (1 / 3), name=f"{short(country)}'s production function, A = {A:.2f}",
                             line=dict(color=TEAL, width=3)))
    fig.update_layout(title=f"{short(country)}: {k ** (1 / 3):.0%} of U.S. income with U.S. TFP, {y:.0%} with its own (A = {A:.2f})",
                      xaxis_range=[0, max(1.3, 1.2 * k)],
                      yaxis=dict(range=[0, 1.6], tickvals=[0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0, 1.25, 1.5]))   # no tick in the corner
    return fig
```

- Choose Japan: it has almost as much capital per person as the United States, but much lower TFP.

### Fig. 7: Measuring TFP so the model fits exactly

**Goal.** See how TFP varies across all 110 countries, and over time.

We plot implied TFP against income, both on ratio scales. Press the play button to move through the
years. Capital per person in the earliest years depends heavily on a starting guess, so we begin in 1980.

> **Python note.** `animation_frame="year"` draws one chart per year and adds a play button and a slider.
> `range_x` and `range_y` fix the axes, so that the points move but the axes do not.

```{python}
years = pwt[pwt.in_sample & pwt.year.isin([1980, 1990, 2000, 2010, 2019, 2023])]
years = years[years.country != "Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of)"]
fig = px.scatter(years, x="y_rel", y="tfp", hover_name="country", animation_frame="year",
                 log_x=True, log_y=True, range_x=[1 / 110, 2.5], range_y=[1 / 40, 2.5],
                 labels={"y_rel": "Per capita GDP (U.S. = 1, ratio scale)",
                         "tfp": "Implied TFP (U.S. = 1, ratio scale)", "year": "Year"},
                 title="Rich countries have high TFP; in the poorest it is below 1/10 of the U.S. level")
fig.update_traces(marker=dict(color=TEAL, size=9))
fig.update_xaxes(tickvals=FRACTIONS, ticktext=FRACTION_NAMES)
fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=FRACTIONS, ticktext=FRACTION_NAMES)
fig.show()
```

**Sources.** Data: [Penn World Table 11.0](https://www.rug.nl/ggdc/productivity/pwt/), Groningen Growth and Development Centre ([DOI 10.34894/FABVLR](https://doi.org/10.34894/FABVLR)), variables `rgdpo` (real GDP), `pop` (population) and `csh_i` (investment share); cite as Feenstra, Inklaar and Timmer (2015), ["The Next Generation of the Penn World Table"](https://doi.org/10.1257/aer.20130954), *American Economic Review* 105(10). Capital per person is our own perpetual-inventory estimate from PWT investment, and TFP is computed from it.
Prepared file: [`data/ch04/pwt_production.csv`](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch04/pwt_production.csv) (see the [data notes](https://github.com/quarcs-lab/macro102-site/blob/main/data/ch04/README.md)).
Chart: inspired by Fig. 4.7 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

**What to notice.**

- The points form a tight upward cloud: rich countries have high TFP, and poor countries have low TFP.
- The differences are large. In the poorest countries TFP is less than 1/10 of the U.S. level.
- Hover over the top right: Ireland, Norway, Singapore and Switzerland all have higher TFP than the
  United States. A few countries, such as Egypt and Syria, have high TFP for their income level.

#### Table 4.4: implied TFP for the textbook's countries

Per capita GDP equals $\bar{k}^{1/3}$ times implied TFP. The textbook's values for 2019 are in the last column.

```{python}
table_4_4 = pd.DataFrame({
    "observed y": y2019.y_rel,
    "k^(1/3)": y2019.k_rel ** (1 / 3),
    "implied TFP": y2019.tfp,
    "textbook: implied TFP": [1.000, 1.054, 0.654, 0.703, 0.721, 0.792, 0.402, 0.347, 0.365, 0.247, 0.074],
})
table_4_4.round(3)
```

#### Key numbers: capital or TFP?

Equation (7) splits the income gap between two countries into a TFP part and a capital part (equation 9):

$$\frac{y^*_{rich}}{y^*_{poor}} = \frac{\bar{A}_{rich}}{\bar{A}_{poor}} \times \left(\frac{\bar{k}_{rich}}{\bar{k}_{poor}}\right)^{1/3}$$

The textbook compares the five richest and the five poorest countries in 2019: incomes differ by a factor
of 75, capital explains a factor of about 5 and TFP a factor of about 15. We redo the calculation for 2023.

```{python}
ranked = sample.sort_values("y_rel")
poorest, richest = ranked.head(5), ranked.tail(5)
income_ratio = richest.y_rel.mean() / poorest.y_rel.mean()
capital_factor = (richest.k_rel.mean() / poorest.k_rel.mean()) ** (1 / 3)
tfp_factor = income_ratio / capital_factor                     # whatever capital does not explain
print("Five richest:", ", ".join(richest.country))
print("Five poorest:", ", ".join(poorest.country))
print(f"Income ratio, rich / poor:   {income_ratio:.0f}")
print(f"Factor explained by capital: {capital_factor:.1f}")
print(f"Factor explained by TFP:     {tfp_factor:.1f}")
```

Our income ratio for 2023 is a little larger than the textbook's 75 for 2019. The split is very close: capital explains a factor of about 5, and TFP about three times as
much. In logarithms, capital explains a bit more than one-third of the gap
($\log 5.2 / \log 82 \approx 0.37$).

We can do the same for Burundi and the United States. With capital differences only, Burundi's income
would be $\bar{k}^{1/3}$ of the U.S. level. With TFP differences only, it would be its TFP.

```{python}
burundi = sample[sample.country == "Burundi"].iloc[0]
capital_only, tfp_only = burundi.k_rel ** (1 / 3), burundi.tfp
print(f"Actual income relative to the U.S.: 1/{1 / burundi.y_rel:.0f}")
print(f"With capital differences only:      1/{1 / capital_only:.1f}")
print(f"With TFP differences only:          1/{1 / tfp_only:.1f}")
print(f"Share of the (log) gap due to capital: {np.log(capital_only) / np.log(burundi.y_rel):.0%}")
```

> **Python note.** `np.log` is the natural logarithm. Because $y = \bar{A}\bar{k}^{1/3}$, the logarithm of $y$
> is the sum of two parts, $\log \bar{A} + \log \bar{k}^{1/3}$, which lets us split the gap into shares.

## Reform and growth: China and Russia

Two large economies changed their institutions after 1990 in very different ways. We compare how their incomes moved since then.

<!-- cell -->

### Fig. 8: Per capita GDP in China and Russia

**Goal.** Compare two very different paths of economic reform after 1990.

Russia reformed quickly, a "big bang" that swept away the old institutions at once. China reformed
gradually. The figure shows what happened to income per person.

> **Python note.** A `SelectMultiple` widget is a list from which you can pick several entries:
> hold Ctrl (or Cmd on a Mac) while clicking. It gives back a tuple of the chosen countries, in the order of
> the list. The loop computes each country's average growth from its first to its last year, and
> `", ".join(parts[:2])` glues the first two results into the title.

```{python}
RATIO_TICKS = [100, 200, 500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000, 20000, 50000, 100000, 200000]


def income_paths(countries=("China", "Russian Federation"), scale="linear"):
    """Fig. 4.9: GDP per person since 1990 for the chosen countries (2021 dollars)."""
    chosen = pwt[pwt.country.isin(countries) & (pwt.year >= 1990)].dropna(subset=["gdp_pc"])
    fig = px.line(chosen, x="year", y="gdp_pc", color="country", log_y=(scale == "ratio"),
                  color_discrete_map=COLORS, category_orders={"country": list(countries)},
                  labels={"gdp_pc": "Per capita GDP (2021 dollars)", "year": "Year", "country": "Country"})
    fig.update_traces(line_width=3)
    parts, missing = [], []
    for name in countries:
        one = chosen[chosen.country == name]
        if len(one) > 1:
            years = one.year.iloc[-1] - one.year.iloc[0]
            growth = round(100 * ((one.gdp_pc.iloc[-1] / one.gdp_pc.iloc[0]) ** (1 / years) - 1), 1) + 0.0
            parts.append(f"{short(name)} {growth:+.1f}%")
        else:
            missing.append(short(name))
    title = "Growth of GDP per person a year since 1990: " + ", ".join(parts[:2])   # the first two countries
    if missing or not parts:
        title = f"No data since 1990 for {', '.join(missing) or 'the chosen countries'}"
    fig.update_layout(title=title, xaxis=dict(range=[1990, 2023], tickvals=[1995, 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020]))
    if scale == "ratio":
        fig.update_yaxes(tickvals=RATIO_TICKS)
    return fig
```

```{python}
#| kind: widget
interact(income_paths,
         countries=SelectMultiple(options=sorted(pwt.country.unique()), value=("China", "Russian Federation"),
                                  rows=8, description="countries", style=WIDE),
         scale=ToggleButtons(options=["linear", "ratio"], description="vertical scale"));
```

```{python}

fig.update_layout(title=income_paths().layout.title.text)           # the title of the textbook view
fig.update_layout(updatemenus=[dict(type="buttons", direction="right", x=0.01, y=0.98, xanchor="left", yanchor="top", buttons=[
    dict(label="linear scale", method="relayout", args=[{"yaxis.type": "linear", "yaxis.autorange": True,
                                                         "yaxis.tickvals": None}]),

                                                        "yaxis.tickvals": RATIO_TICKS}])])])
country_menu(fig, ["China", "Russian Federation"], regions.set_index("country").region)

GDP per person is `rgdpo` / `pop`, in 2021 dollars. ## Concluding remarks

- The **Cobb-Douglas production function**, equation (1), $Y = \bar{A}K^{1/3}L^{2/3}$, has constant returns to
  scale but a **diminishing marginal product** of each input on its own, equations (2) and (3).
- Firms hire each input until its marginal product equals its price. In equilibrium, equation (4), all
  capital and labor are employed, $r^* = \frac{1}{3}\bar{A}(\bar{L}/\bar{K})^{2/3}$ and $w^* = \frac{2}{3}\bar{A}(\bar{K}/\bar{L})^{1/3}$.
  Capital earns one-third of output and labor two-thirds, whatever the amounts of capital and labor
  (equation 5), and payments exhaust output, so profit is zero (equation 6).
- Per person, the model says $y^* = \bar{A}\bar{k}^{1/3}$, equation (7). With equal productivity, it predicts much
  smaller income gaps than we see, because of diminishing returns to capital.
- Measured as the residual that makes the model fit, equation (8), **TFP** differs enormously across
  countries. The split of income gaps in equation (9) shows that it explains most of the gap between rich
  and poor, roughly two-thirds to three-quarters of it.
- The production model takes capital as given. The next chapter, on the **Solow model**, explains where
  capital per person comes from.

### Conceptual problems

<!-- cell -->

**Problem 1 (Basic): The U.S. economy through the lens of the model.** In 2024, U.S. GDP was 29,381 billion dollars ([U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, Gross Domestic Product (`GDPA`), via FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/GDPA)), and on average 161.3 million people had a job (the mean of the twelve monthly values of the [U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Employment Level (`CE16OV`), via FRED](https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/CE16OV)). Treat GDP as the model's output $Y$ and employment as its labor $L$.

(a) According to the factor shares of equation (5), how much of this income went to labor, and how much to capital?

(b) What average wage per worker does the hiring rule for labor, equation (3), imply? Give two reasons why it is higher than the pay that a typical worker sees on a paycheck.

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

Labor gets two-thirds of output and capital one-third. Equation (3) says $w = \frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{Y}{L}$: first compute output per worker, then take two-thirds of it. Think about what the model counts as "labor income", and about the difference between an average and a typical value.

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

(a) By equation (5), labor receives $w^*L^*/Y^* = 2/3$ of output and capital $r^*K^*/Y^* = 1/3$:

$$w^*L^* = \tfrac{2}{3}\times 29{,}381 \approx 19{,}587 \text{ billion dollars}, \qquad r^*K^* = \tfrac{1}{3}\times 29{,}381 \approx 9{,}794 \text{ billion dollars}.$$

That is about \$19.6 trillion for workers and \$9.8 trillion for the owners of capital. The two add up to GDP, as equation (6) says.

(b) Output per worker is $Y/L = 29{,}381\text{ billion} / 161.348\text{ million} \approx 182{,}097$ dollars a year. The hiring rule gives

$$w^* = \frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{Y}{L} \approx \frac{2}{3}\times 182{,}097 \approx 121{,}398 \text{ dollars a year}.$$

A typical paycheck is smaller for two reasons. First, the model's wage is *all* labor income per worker: it includes what employers pay for health insurance, pensions and payroll taxes, which never appear in take-home pay. Second, it is an *average*, and a few very high earners pull an average up; the typical (median) worker earns less than the average worker. The model has one kind of worker, so it cannot tell these apart.

```python
Y_us, L_us = 29380.991e9, 161.348e6        # 2024 GDP in dollars and employment in people
print(f"(a) labor income {2 / 3 * Y_us / 1e9:,.0f} billion, capital income {Y_us / 3 / 1e9:,.0f} billion")
print(f"(b) output per worker {Y_us / L_us:,.0f} dollars; model wage w* = {2 / 3 * Y_us / L_us:,.0f} dollars")
```

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Problem 2 (Intermediate): Misallocation lowers measured TFP.** A hypothetical country has two ice-cream firms with the same technology, $Y_i = K_i^{1/3}L_i^{2/3}$ with $\bar{A} = 1$, and one worker each. The country owns 8 machines. The old firm belongs to a well-connected family and gets cheap loans, so it runs 7 machines; a new start-up gets only 1.

(a) Compute each firm's output and total output.

(b) Compute each firm's marginal product of capital with equation (2). Which firm would add more output with one extra machine?

(c) Move the machines one at a time from the old firm to the start-up. Which split of the 8 machines gives the most output, and by what percent does total output rise compared with (a)?

(d) An economist sees only the totals: 8 machines, 2 workers and the output of (a). She measures TFP with equation (8), applied to the whole economy. What TFP does she find? Why would a competitive capital market, in which every firm pays the same rental price, avoid this loss? [Hsieh and Klenow (2009)](https://doi.org/10.1162/qjec.2009.124.4.1403) estimate that if capital and labor were spread across plants as evenly as in the United States, judged by their marginal products, manufacturing TFP would rise by 30 to 50 percent in China and by 40 to 60 percent in India.

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

With one worker, a firm's output is just $K_i^{1/3}$, and its MPK is $\frac{1}{3}K_i^{-2/3}$. For (d), the whole economy's TFP is total output divided by $K^{1/3}L^{2/3}$ with $K = 8$ and $L = 2$. For the last question, recall the hiring rule for capital in each firm.

</details>

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<!-- cell -->

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

(a) The old firm makes $7^{1/3} \approx 1.913$ tons and the start-up $1^{1/3} = 1$ ton, so total output is about $2.913$ tons.

(b) By equation (2) with $L_i = 1$, $MPK_i = \frac{1}{3}K_i^{-2/3}$. For the old firm, $\frac{1}{3}\times 7^{-2/3} \approx 0.091$; for the start-up, $\frac{1}{3}\times 1^{-2/3} \approx 0.333$. One more machine adds almost four times as much output at the start-up.

(c) Output for each split:

| Machines, old firm and start-up | Total output | MPK, old firm | MPK, start-up |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7 and 1 | 2.913 | 0.091 | 0.333 |
| 6 and 2 | 3.077 | 0.101 | 0.210 |
| 5 and 3 | 3.152 | 0.114 | 0.160 |
| 4 and 4 | 3.175 | 0.132 | 0.132 |

Output is largest with 4 machines in each firm, where the two marginal products are equal. It rises from 2.913 to 3.175 tons, by about 9.0 percent, with the same machines and workers.

(d) For the whole economy, $K^{1/3}L^{2/3} = 8^{1/3}\times 2^{2/3} = 2\times 2^{2/3} \approx 3.175$. The measured TFP is

$$\bar{A} = \frac{2.913}{3.175} \approx 0.918,$$

about 8.2 percent below the true productivity of each firm, $\bar{A} = 1$. Nothing is wrong with the technology: the loss comes from where the machines are. In a competitive market, each firm rents machines until $MPK_i = r$. With one rental price for everybody, the marginal products are equal, and with the same technology and the same labor that means the same number of machines in each firm: the efficient split. Cheap loans for the connected firm lower its cost of capital below $r$, so it keeps renting machines whose marginal product is low. Measured TFP, a residual, records the loss as lower productivity. Hsieh and Klenow's estimates suggest that in China and India this kind of loss is large.

```python
for K_old, K_new in [(7, 1), (6, 2), (5, 3), (4, 4)]:
    Y_total = production(K_old, 1) + production(K_new, 1)          # one worker in each firm
    print(f"{K_old} and {K_new} machines: output {Y_total:.3f};  MPK {mpk(K_old, 1):.3f} and {mpk(K_new, 1):.3f}")
Y_total = production(7, 1) + production(1, 1)
print(f"Measured TFP with 7 and 1 machines: {Y_total / production(8, 2):.3f}")
```

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Problem 3 (Challenge): Why does Ireland top the TFP ranking?** In our data for 2023, Ireland has the highest implied TFP of the 110 countries of Fig. 7, 1.50 times the U.S. level, with income per person 1.82 times and capital per person 1.77 times the U.S. level. Much of Ireland's GDP, however, is income of multinational firms that have moved their headquarters, their patents and other intellectual property, or their fleets of leased aircraft to Ireland. Ireland's Central Statistics Office therefore publishes a second measure, modified gross national income (GNI\*), which starts from GDP and takes out the profits that these firms send abroad, the income of relocated headquarters, and the depreciation of their intellectual property and leased aircraft: in 2023 it was 55.5 percent of GDP ([CSO, Annual National Accounts 2024](https://www.cso.ie/en/releasesandpublications/ep/p-ana/annualnationalaccounts2024/gniandde-globalisedresults/)).

(a) Use equation (8) to explain why the measured TFP rises one for one with any overstatement of output. Besides efficiency, what else can end up in this residual?

(b) Suppose GNI\* measures Ireland's income better than GDP, so that income per person is 55.5 percent of the measured value, while capital per person stays at 1.77. Treat U.S. GDP as a good measure of U.S. income. What are Ireland's income per person and TFP relative to the United States now?

(c) The same firms' patents and aircraft are also counted in Ireland's capital stock. Suppose, hypothetically, that Ireland's true capital per person is only half the measured value. Recompute TFP with the income of (b). Which mistake moves measured TFP more, an error in output or an error in capital, and why?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

Equation (8) is $\bar{A} = y/\bar{k}^{1/3}$, so the elasticity of measured TFP is $1$ with respect to $y$ and $-1/3$ with respect to $\bar{k}$. In (b), multiply $y$ by 0.555 and keep $\bar{k}$; in (c), also multiply $\bar{k}$ by 0.5.

</details>

<!-- cell -->

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

(a) TFP is not observed: it is whatever makes equation (7) hold, $\bar{A} = y/\bar{k}^{1/3}$. If measured output is 10 percent too high, measured TFP is 10 percent too high as well, since $y$ enters with an exponent of 1. So the residual collects everything that raises measured income per person for given capital: true efficiency, but also natural resources (oil, gas, minerals), human capital, and plain measurement problems such as profits that firms book in a country for tax reasons.

(b) Income per person becomes $1.818\times 0.555 \approx 1.009$ times the U.S. level, about the same as the United States. Because $\bar{k}$ does not change, TFP falls in the same proportion:

$$\bar{A} = 1.502\times 0.555 \approx 0.834.$$

With this TFP, Ireland would rank 13th of the 110 countries instead of first, between Austria and Sweden.

(c) Halving capital per person multiplies $\bar{k}^{1/3}$ by $0.5^{1/3} \approx 0.794$, so TFP is divided by 0.794, that is, multiplied by $0.5^{-1/3} \approx 1.260$:

$$\bar{A} = \frac{1.009}{(0.5\times 1.773)^{1/3}} \approx 1.051.$$

The output error matters much more. Cutting output by 44.5 percent cut TFP by 44.5 percent, while halving capital raised TFP by only 26 percent, because capital enters with an exponent of only $1/3$. Development accounting is therefore most sensitive to how we measure GDP. Ireland is the extreme case of a general lesson: before reading a country's TFP as "efficiency", check what its GDP measures.

</details>

**Problem 4 (Basic): Is capital more unequal than income?** Load this chapter's [Penn World Table 11.0](https://www.rug.nl/ggdc/productivity/pwt/) data, `pwt_production.csv`, and keep the 110 countries of Fig. 5 in 2023 (the rows with `in_sample` true, without Venezuela). # Your answer here

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

We filter the year and the sample, then divide the two percentiles of each column.

```python
panel = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "pwt_production.csv")
cross = panel[(panel.year == 2023) & panel.in_sample]
cross = cross[cross.country != "Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of)"]      # implausible GDP, as in Fig. 5
for column in ["k_rel", "y_rel"]:
    ratio = cross[column].quantile(0.9) / cross[column].quantile(0.1)
    print(f"{column}: 90th / 10th percentile = {ratio:.1f}")
k_ratio = cross.k_rel.quantile(0.9) / cross.k_rel.quantile(0.1)
print(f"Predicted income ratio with equal TFP: {k_ratio ** (1 / 3):.2f}")
```

The country at the 90th percentile has 53.5 times the capital per person of the country at the 10th percentile, but only 24.2 times its income. Capital is about twice as unequal as income. With equal TFP, though, the model predicts an income ratio of only $53.5^{1/3} \approx 3.77$, because of the strong diminishing returns to capital. The actual income ratio is more than six times larger than that, so most of the income differences must come from TFP.

</details>

**Problem 5 (Intermediate): Catching up: capital or TFP?** Between 1980 and 2023, China's income per person rose from about 3 percent to 30 percent of the U.S. level. Equation (9) splits a change over time just as it splits a gap between two countries: the change in the log of relative income equals the change in the log of relative TFP plus one-third of the change in the log of relative capital per person. For China, South Korea (`Republic of Korea` in the data), Indonesia and Mexico, compute these three changes from 1980 to 2023, and the share of the income change that comes from capital. Which country's catch-up relied most on capital? What happened in Mexico?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

For one country, `one = panel[panel.country == "China"].set_index("year")` lets you write `one.y_rel[2023]`. The income change is `np.log(one.y_rel[2023] / one.y_rel[1980])`; the capital part divides the log change of `k_rel` by 3, and the TFP part is the log change of `tfp`. A loop over the four names prints one line per country.

</details>

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

For each country we take logs of the 2023/1980 ratios. The capital and TFP parts add up to the income change.

```python
panel = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "pwt_production.csv")
print("country             income  capital  TFP    capital share")
for name in ["China", "Republic of Korea", "Indonesia", "Mexico"]:
    one = panel[panel.country == name].set_index("year")
    income = np.log(one.y_rel[2023] / one.y_rel[1980])          # change in log relative income
    capital = np.log(one.k_rel[2023] / one.k_rel[1980]) / 3     # one-third of the capital change
    tfp = np.log(one.tfp[2023] / one.tfp[1980])                 # change in log relative TFP
    print(f"{name:18s} {income:6.2f} {capital:8.2f} {tfp:6.2f} {capital / income:9.2f}")
```

| Country | Income change (log) | Capital part | TFP part | Capital share |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| China | 2.35 | 0.85 | 1.50 | 0.36 |
| South Korea | 1.49 | 0.68 | 0.81 | 0.46 |
| Indonesia | 0.94 | 0.69 | 0.25 | 0.73 |
| Mexico | −0.54 | −0.02 | −0.52 | 0.04 |

China's relative income rose by a factor of about $e^{2.35} \approx 10.5$. Capital explains about a third of this rise in logs and TFP about two-thirds, close to the split of the gap between rich and poor countries in the Key numbers after Fig. 7. Indonesia relied most on capital: almost three-quarters of its catch-up came from accumulating machines and buildings, and its TFP rose only a little relative to the United States. Mexico fell *behind*: its income per person dropped from 47 to 27 percent of the U.S. level, and almost all of the fall, 96 percent of it in logs, came from relative TFP, while its relative capital barely changed.

</details>

**Problem 6 (Challenge): Where does capital earn the most?** [Lucas (1990)](https://ideas.repec.org/a/aea/aecrev/v80y1990i2p92-96.html) asked why so little capital flows from rich to poor countries. If India and the United States differed only in capital, he showed, the marginal product of capital in India would have to be about 58 times the U.S. one ([Alfaro, Kalemli-Ozcan and Volosovych 2005](https://www.nber.org/papers/w11901)). Check this puzzle with our data for 2023, using the 110 countries of Fig. 5 without the United States.

(a) Equation (2) per person reads $MPK = \frac{1}{3}y/\bar{k}$. Show that a country's MPK relative to the United States is $y_{rel}/k_{rel}$, and that with equal TFP it would be $k_{rel}^{-2/3}$.

(b) Compute both for each country. Merge in the income groups of `regions.csv` (from the [World Bank country and lending groups](https://datahelpdesk.worldbank.org/knowledgebase/articles/906519-world-bank-country-and-lending-groups)) and report the median of each measure by income group.

(c) Where is the return to capital highest? How does the measured gap compare with the gap the model predicts under equal TFP, and what does this suggest about Lucas's puzzle?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

(a) Divide the MPK of country $i$ by the U.S. MPK: the $\frac{1}{3}$ cancels. Then replace $y_{rel}$ with $k_{rel}^{1/3}$. (b) `cross.merge(groups[["country", "income_group"]], on="country")` adds the income group to each row, and `.groupby("income_group")[[...]].median()` gives a table of medians.

</details>

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

(a) For country $i$ and the United States,

$$\frac{MPK_i}{MPK_{US}} = \frac{\frac{1}{3}\,y_i/\bar{k}_i}{\frac{1}{3}\,y_{US}/\bar{k}_{US}} = \frac{y_i/y_{US}}{\bar{k}_i/\bar{k}_{US}} = \frac{y_{rel}}{k_{rel}}.$$

With equal TFP, equation (7) gives $y_{rel} = k_{rel}^{1/3}$, so $MPK_{rel} = k_{rel}^{1/3}/k_{rel} = k_{rel}^{-2/3}$. A country with 1/8 of U.S. capital per person would then earn $8^{2/3} = 4$ times the U.S. return.

(b) We build both columns, merge the income groups and take medians.

```python
panel = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "pwt_production.csv")
groups = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "regions.csv")
cross = panel[(panel.year == 2023) & panel.in_sample]
cross = cross[(cross.country != "Venezuela (Bolivarian Republic of)") & (cross.country != "United States")]
cross = cross.merge(groups[["country", "income_group"]], on="country")
cross["mpk_equal_tfp"] = cross.k_rel ** (-2 / 3)              # MPK relative to the U.S. with U.S. TFP
cross["mpk_measured"] = cross.y_rel / cross.k_rel             # with each country's own TFP
order = ["Low income", "Lower middle income", "Upper middle income", "High income"]
table = cross.groupby("income_group")[["mpk_equal_tfp", "mpk_measured"]].median()
print(table.loc[order].round(2))
print(cross.groupby("income_group").size().loc[order])
```

| Income group (countries) | MPK relative to the U.S., equal TFP | MPK relative to the U.S., measured |
|---|---|---|
| Low income (16) | 16.20 | 2.03 |
| Lower middle income (28) | 7.77 | 1.34 |
| Upper middle income (28) | 3.10 | 1.23 |
| High income (37) | 1.12 | 0.89 |

(c) The return to capital is highest in the low-income countries, and it falls with income in both columns, so the model points the right way: capital should flow toward poor countries. But the size is very different. With equal TFP, the typical low-income country would earn 16 times the U.S. return; with its own, much lower TFP, it earns only about twice the U.S. return. Low TFP makes each machine less productive, and that removes most of the reason to move capital, which goes a long way toward solving Lucas's puzzle. The remaining gap may reflect risk and weak institutions: Alfaro, Kalemli-Ozcan and Volosovych find that in 1970–2000 low institutional quality, for example poorly protected property rights, was the leading explanation of why so little capital flows to poor countries. Keep in mind that our capital stocks are estimates built from past investment, so the numbers for single countries are rough.

</details>

### Modeling problems

**Problem 7 (Basic): An investment tax credit.** A hypothetical ice-cream firm with 64 workers already rents 7 machines, and a machine rents for 1.5 tons of ice cream a year. The firm follows the hiring rule: it rents another machine only if the machine adds at least as much output as its rent. The slider below draws the firm's production function of Fig. 1, and the title reports the output gain from the 8th machine.

(a) Does the firm rent the 8th machine?

(b) The government introduces an investment tax credit that cuts the firm's cost of renting a machine to 1.3 tons a year. Does the firm now rent the 8th machine?

(c) Move the workers slider. What is the smallest workforce on the slider at which the 8th machine pays for itself, without the credit and with it?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

Compare the second number in the title, the gain "from K = 7 to 8", with the cost of a machine. More workers make each machine more productive, so the gain grows as you move the slider to the right.

</details>

```{python}
#| kind: widget
interact(production_curve,
         L=FloatSlider(value=64, min=40, max=96, step=8, description="workers L", style=WIDE),
         A=fixed(1.0), alpha=fixed(1 / 3));
```

**Source.** The model of Fig. 1 above, adapted from Fig. 4.1 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

(a) With 64 workers, the 8th machine adds 1.39 tons, less than its rent of 1.5 tons. The firm does not rent it: it would lose about 0.11 tons a year.

(b) With the credit, the machine costs 1.3 tons, less than the 1.39 tons it adds. Now the firm rents it. By lowering the cost of capital, the credit moves the firm down its demand curve for capital, to more machines.

(c) The gain from the 8th machine rises with the workforce:

| Workers | 48 | 56 | 64 | 72 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gain from the 8th machine (tons) | 1.15 | 1.27 | 1.39 | 1.51 |

Without the credit, the smallest workforce on the slider for which the machine pays is 72 workers, where it adds 1.51 tons. With the credit, 64 workers are enough, while at 56 workers the gain of 1.27 tons is still below 1.3. The policy lowers the bar for investment, and firms with fewer workers start to invest too. One caution: in the economy as a whole, the supply of machines is fixed in this model, so a credit given to every firm would mostly push up the rental price that machine owners receive. The number of machines grows only as people invest over time, the subject of the Solow model in Chapter 5.

```python
for L_firm in [48, 56, 64, 72]:
    gain = production(8, L_firm) - production(7, L_firm)        # extra output from the 8th machine
    print(f"{L_firm} workers: the 8th machine adds {gain:.2f} tons")
```

</details>

**Problem 8 (Intermediate): Investment program or productivity reform?** A finance minister must choose between two plans for an economy that starts at the baseline of Fig. 2, $\bar{K} = \bar{L} = \bar{A} = 1$. Plan (i) is an investment program that raises the capital stock by 30 percent. Plan (ii) is a reform package (less red tape and more competition, say) that raises productivity $\bar{A}$ by 10 percent. The number of workers does not change.

(a) Which plan raises the wage more? Set the sliders for each plan and read $w^*$ in the title.

(b) What happens to the rental price $r^*$ under each plan? And to the total income of capital owners, $r^*\bar{K}$?

(c) How large would the investment program have to be to raise the wage as much as the reform? Bracket the answer with the slider, then compute it with equation (4).

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

Plan (i) is $\bar{K} = 1.3$ with $\bar{A} = 1$; plan (ii) is $\bar{K} = 1$ with $\bar{A} = 1.1$. By equation (4), the wage has an elasticity of $1/3$ with respect to $\bar{K}$ and of $1$ with respect to $\bar{A}$. For (c), solve $\bar{K}^{1/3} = 1.1$.

</details>

```{python}
#| kind: widget
interact(factor_markets,
         K_bar=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=1.0, max=1.5, step=0.1, description="supply of capital K̄", style=WIDE),
         A=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=1.0, max=1.2, step=0.05, description="productivity A", style=WIDE),
         L_bar=fixed(1.0), alpha=fixed(1 / 3));
```

**Source.** The model of Fig. 2 above, adapted from Fig. 4.2 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

(a) At the baseline, $w^* = 0.667$ and $r^* = 0.333$. Plan (i) raises the wage to $w^* = \frac{2}{3}\times 1.3^{1/3} \approx 0.728$, by 9.1 percent. Plan (ii) raises it to $w^* = \frac{2}{3}\times 1.1 \approx 0.733$, by 10 percent. The reform raises the wage slightly more, although it changes its parameter by only a third as much.

(b) Under plan (i), the rental price *falls*, to $r^* = \frac{1}{3}\times 1.3^{-2/3} \approx 0.280$, by 16.0 percent: more machines means a lower marginal product of each one. Under plan (ii), the rental price *rises* by 10 percent, to 0.367. Total capital income still rises under both plans, because it is always one-third of output (equation 5): $r^*\bar{K} \approx 0.280\times 1.3 \approx 0.364$ under plan (i), a rise of 9.1 percent, and $0.367$ under plan (ii), a rise of 10 percent. Workers and capital owners both gain from either plan, but the reform raises everything, while the investment program lowers the return on each machine.

(c) The wage is proportional to $\bar{A}\bar{K}^{1/3}$. To match a 10 percent rise in $\bar{A}$ with capital alone, $\bar{K}^{1/3} = 1.1$, so $\bar{K} = 1.1^3 \approx 1.331$: the capital stock would have to rise by 33.1 percent. On the slider, $\bar{K} = 1.3$ gives a slightly lower wage than the reform, and $\bar{K} = 1.4$ a higher one. Because of diminishing returns, a 1 percent rise in TFP is worth a 3 percent rise in the capital stock. The policy lesson is not that investment is useless, but that reforms which raise productivity can be worth a great deal of capital, and they usually cost far less than building it.

```python
for K_plan, A_plan in [(1.0, 1.0), (1.3, 1.0), (1.0, 1.1), (1.331, 1.0)]:
    w_plan, r_plan = mpl(K_plan, 1, A_plan), mpk(K_plan, 1, A_plan)
    print(f"K = {K_plan}, A = {A_plan}:  w* = {w_plan:.3f},  r* = {r_plan:.3f},  r*K = {r_plan * K_plan:.3f}")
```

</details>

**Problem 9 (Challenge): How can India double its relative income?** In our data for 2023, India's income per person is 12.3 percent of the U.S. level, its capital per person 9.4 percent and its TFP 0.27. Suppose the government sets the goal of doubling income per person relative to the United States, to about 24.6 percent. The sliders below multiply India's capital per person and its TFP, and draw the result on the production functions of Fig. 6.

(a) With today's TFP, by what factor must capital per person rise to reach the goal?

(b) With today's capital, by what factor must TFP rise?

(c) Hsieh and Klenow (2009), quoted in Problem 2, estimate that cutting misallocation to the U.S. level could raise TFP in Indian manufacturing by 40 to 60 percent. Suppose a reform raised India's TFP by 40 percent in the whole economy. By what factor would capital per person still have to rise to reach the goal?

(d) Capital follows productivity. In an open economy, investors add machines until the MPK is back at the return they can earn elsewhere. With the per-person MPK, $\frac{1}{3}\bar{A}\bar{k}^{-2/3}$, find by what factor capital per person rises after the 40 percent TFP gain if the MPK returns to its old value. How far does India then get toward its goal?

(e) Choose another country in the menu. Do your answers to (a) and (b) change? What would you tell a government that can fund either a large investment program or a productivity reform?

<details><summary>Hint</summary>

Equation (7) says $y = \bar{A}\bar{k}^{1/3}$, so the factor by which $y$ rises is the TFP factor times the cube root of the capital factor. In each part, write that product and set it equal to 2. In (d), write the MPK before and after the reform, and set the two equal.

</details>

```{python}
#| kind: widget
def reform_chart(country="India", capital=1.0, tfp=1.0):
    """Fig. 6 after a policy that multiplies capital per person and TFP (equation 7)."""
    fig = compare_with_us(country)
    row = sample[sample.country == country].iloc[0]
    k_new, A_new = capital * row.k_rel, tfp * row.tfp
    y_new = A_new * k_new ** (1 / 3)                                    # equation (7)
    grid = np.linspace(0, 2, 300)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=grid, y=A_new * grid ** (1 / 3), name=f"After the policy, A = {A_new:.2f}",
                             mode="lines", line=dict(color=GREEN, width=3, dash="dash")))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[k_new], y=[y_new], name="After the policy", mode="markers",
                             marker=dict(color=GREEN, size=15, symbol="star")))
    fig.update_layout(title=f"{short(country)}: {y_new:.1%} of U.S. income after the policy, "
                            f"{row.y_rel:.1%} today ({y_new / row.y_rel:.2f} times)")
    return fig


interact(reform_chart,
         country=Dropdown(options=["India", "Bangladesh", "Pakistan", "Nigeria"], value="India",
                          description="country", style=WIDE),
         capital=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=1.0, max=8.0, step=0.5, description="capital per person ×", style=WIDE),
         tfp=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=1.0, max=2.0, step=0.1, description="TFP ×", style=WIDE));
```

**Source.** The model of Fig. 6 above, with each country's 2023 numbers from the Penn World Table 11.0 (`pwt_production.csv`), adapted from Fig. 4.6 in Jones (2024), [*Macroeconomics*, 6th ed.](https://wwnorton.com/books/9781324063612)

```{python}
# Your answer here
```

**Your answer:**

<!-- cell -->

<details><summary>Solution</summary>

(a) With $\bar{A}$ fixed, $y$ doubles only if $\bar{k}^{1/3}$ doubles, so $\bar{k}$ must rise by a factor of $2^3 = 8$: from 9.4 to about 75 percent of U.S. capital per person. Set capital to 8 and the title shows 24.6 percent, 2.00 times today's income.

(b) With $\bar{k}$ fixed, $\bar{A}$ must double, from 0.27 to 0.54. Set TFP to 2 and the title again shows 2.00 times.

(c) The reform supplies a factor of 1.4, so capital must supply the rest: $\bar{k}^{1/3}$ must rise by $2/1.4 \approx 1.43$, and $\bar{k}$ by

$$\left(\frac{2}{1.4}\right)^3 \approx 2.92.$$

On the sliders, TFP at 1.4 with capital at 2.5 falls just short of the goal, and capital at 3 just reaches it. A productivity reform cuts the capital India needs from 8 times to about 3 times today's level.

(d) If the MPK returns to its old value, $\bar{A}\bar{k}^{-2/3}$ is unchanged. With $\bar{A}' = 1.4\bar{A}$,

$$1.4\,\bar{A}\,(\bar{k}')^{-2/3} = \bar{A}\,\bar{k}^{-2/3} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{\bar{k}'}{\bar{k}} = 1.4^{3/2} \approx 1.657.$$

Income then rises by $1.4\times 1.657^{1/3} = 1.4\times 1.4^{1/2} = 1.4^{3/2} \approx 1.657$, that is, by 65.7 percent rather than 40 percent. India would reach about 20.3 percent of U.S. income, most of the way to its goal of 24.6 percent. The same exponent $3/2$ on $\bar{A}$ appears in the steady state of the Solow model ([Chapter 5](https://quarcs-lab.github.io/macro102-site/notebooks/ch05-the-solow-growth-model.html)), where capital also responds to productivity.

(e) The factors do not change from country to country: 8 for capital alone and 2 for TFP alone, whatever the starting point, because the elasticities of equation (7), $1/3$ for capital and $1$ for TFP, are the same everywhere. For a government the lesson is that capital alone is a very expensive road to higher income, because each extra machine adds less than the one before. A reform that raises TFP pays off twice: directly, and by raising the return to capital, which attracts investment. The hard part is that the model does not say how to raise TFP; that is the question of institutions, technology and misallocation discussed above.

```python
india = sample[sample.country == "India"].iloc[0]
now = india.tfp * india.k_rel ** (1 / 3)                         # equation (7) with today's values
target = 2 * india.y_rel
print(f"(a) capital factor with today's TFP:     {(target / now) ** 3:.2f}")
print(f"(b) TFP factor with today's capital:     {target / now:.2f}")
print(f"(c) capital factor after a 40% TFP gain: {(target / (1.4 * now)) ** 3:.2f}")
print(f"(d) capital and income factor: {1.4 ** 1.5:.3f}; India reaches {1.4 ** 1.5 * india.y_rel:.1%} of U.S. income")
```

</details>
